body: South Africa drives on the left. Note: A handful of other countries also drive on the left.
South Africa uses single yellow outer lines and white centre lines on most roads. Botswana, Eswatini, and Lesotho also use single yellow outer lines; Australia rarely uses them.

South Africa features unique white triple centre lines (two solid outside and one dashed inside) and sometimes a triple line with a yellow middle line; mostly on larger roads. These are also found in Botswana, Eswatini, and Lesotho.
Generation 2 coverage is common in South Africa, identifiable by large circular car blur and sky colour distortion. It is the only African country with Gen 2 coverage.

South Africa has 11 official languages including English, Afrikaans (a Germanic language close to Dutch), and various Bantu languages. English is the lingua franca. Afrikaans is common in the western half and appears in place names nationwide, limiting its use for region guessing. Afrikaans is rare in Eswatini, Lesotho, and Botswana.
Common poles in South Africa have 1 to 5 horizontal bars with thin white insulators resembling rows of birds, called bird poles. The country has diverse poles and pole tops, some regionally unique.
South Africa uses green directional signs with yellow road numbers. Road number formats differ regionally: N and R roads are unique to South Africa.
South Africa uses triangular warning signs with red border and white background. Botswana, Eswatini, and Lesotho use similar signs; Australia and New Zealand use yellow diamond-shaped signs.
South Africa uses white-and-red chevrons. Unique small, thin chevrons with one arrow are common next to roads and also found in Botswana, Eswatini, and Lesotho.
Suburban houses around large cities are often surrounded by high walls, fences, and gates.
All Generation 4 coverage in South Africa was taken by a blue Street View car with a short antenna, sometimes hidden by blur.
South Africa has Generation 4 smallcam coverage with a low-mounted camera and big circular blur, sometimes fully transparent with a short rear antenna.
Each province has a distinct licence plate design, somewhat visible through blur; Free State has a green tint and KwaZulu-Natal a blue tint.
South African major highways show the letter 'N' before numbers on signs; Google Maps shows a blue pentagon instead.
R-roads with three-digit numbers are geographically grouped but can span provinces; 100s are widespread.
Telephone numbers are 10 digits; first three digits denote geographic area. Mobile numbers start with 06–08 and are not area-specific.
Poles with 3 bars forming an 'A' shape are mostly found in Western Cape, rarely in bordering provinces.
Similar poles in Eastern Cape have a wider 'A' shape with bottom insulators attached directly to the shape.
Trident pole tops are almost unique to KwaZulu-Natal.
Poles with 3 alternating horizontal insulators appear mostly in Limpopo, Gauteng, North West, Mpumalanga, and sometimes Northern Cape.
Poles with 2 diagonal bars forming a '<' shape are mostly in northeastern provinces, mainly Limpopo and North West.
Poles with 1 or 2 metal arms holding insulators are common in Mpumalanga.
Square red stickers on the back of regular signs often appear in Eastern Cape and nearby provinces; red stickers on chevrons are widespread.
White stickers on the back of chevrons are common in the Cape provinces.
You can find grainy, almost Texas-like pavement with a pink hint in Limpopo.
Large bird nests on top of poles are common in the northern part of Northern Cape.
Power plants are often seen between Secunda and eMalahleni in Mpumalanga.
Northeast South Africa looks dry and somewhat barren with orange or red soil, hills/mountains covered in shrubs; coverage varies with seasons.
Unique rocky, treeless mountains are found in Western Cape with tall, steep sides and sharp peaks, similar to mountains near Lesotho.
Vineyards are mostly in valleys near the coast of Western Cape and near Upington in Northern Cape.
A dry landscape with red soil is typical in Northern Cape, useful for climate-based guessing.
Sugarcane plantations are mostly in KwaZulu-Natal along the coast, also present in Mpumalanga near Mozambique.
Uniquely tall Cook pine trees are found mostly between East London and Durban; they are planted and may appear elsewhere on the coast.
Pine tree plantations are common west of Eswatini and south in KwaZulu-Natal, and typically seen in Eswatini.
Grassy rolling hills are located in coastal Western Cape between Cape Town and George with tall ridges usually to the north or east.
The landscape near the Mozambique border is noticeably flat with green subtropical vegetation.
A camouflage car with black side mirrors and roof racks appears in Kruger National Park near the Mozambique border; the park has Generation 4 coverage.

Kruger National Park has a flat savannah climate with dry vegetation, grasses, scattered small trees, and red soil. Unique directional waystones mark junctions. Roads are mostly unpaved gravel or small paved roads without lines.
Metropolitan routes marked with 'M' are major roads in cities, with distinct signs in Port Elizabeth (Gqeberha) and Durban.
Traffic lights and pedestrian crossing poles in Johannesburg have three strips of reflective tape.
Durban uniquely features a bump on top of lamps and arms, though the standard design is still seen.
Public infrastructure in Gauteng, especially Johannesburg and Emalahleni, often displays dodgy adverts for abortion services or penis enlargement pills.
North of Bokspits on R360 near Botswana border has reddish asphalt, arid landscape with dry greyish trees, shrubs, and golden grass.
Table Mountain west of Cape Town features a three-kilometre plateau flanked by the pyramidal Devil’s Peak.
Mountains in Witfontein Nature Reserve, likely George’s Peak, are visible north from George.
